Inter-Rater Agreement and Reliability in Pathology

Source: vignettes/03-agreement-analysis.Rmd
03-agreement-analysis.Rmd

This article is a short, practical guide to the Interrater Reliability analysis (agreement(), jamovi menu meddecide > Agreement > Interrater Reliability). It shows which statistic fits which kind of rating, and how to read the result tables from R. For every option, see ?agreement or the comprehensive guide.

Each rater is one column of data; each row is one case. Pass the rater columns to vars. With two raters the analysis reports Cohen’s kappa; with three or more, Fleiss’ kappa.

Choosing a statistic

Ratings Primary statistic Options
Nominal (e.g. diagnosis) Cohen’s / Fleiss’ kappa default; kripp = TRUE, gwet = TRUE
Ordinal (e.g. grade 1-3) Weighted kappa (2 raters); ordinal alpha or Gwet’s AC2 (3+ raters) wght = "equal" (linear) or "squared" (quadratic); with 3+ raters allPairsKappa = TRUE gives weighted kappa per pair, or krippMethod = "ordinal", gwetWeights
Rare category, skewed prevalence Gwet’s AC1, PABAK gwet = TRUE, pabak = TRUE
Continuous (e.g. Ki-67 %) ICC, Lin’s CCC, Bland-Altman icc = TRUE, linCCC = TRUE, blandAltmanPlot = TRUE
Missing ratings, any scale Krippendorff’s alpha kripp = TRUE, krippMethod = "nominal"/"ordinal"/"interval"/"ratio"
Which pairs disagree All-pairs kappa allPairsKappa = TRUE

Nominal ratings: three raters

The bundled histopathology data has three binary rater columns.

data(histopathology)

res <- agreement(
  data = histopathology,
  vars = c("Rater 1", "Rater 2", "Rater 3"),
  kripp = TRUE,
  gwet = TRUE,
  allPairsKappa = TRUE
)

res$irrtable$asDF                          # Fleiss' kappa
#>        method subjects raters peragree     kappa ci_lower  ci_upper        z
#> "1" Fleiss' κ      250      3 76.30522 0.6512801 0.572085 0.7304752 16.19697
#>                p
#> "1" 8.688896e-41
res$krippTableGroup$krippTable$asDF        # Krippendorff's alpha
#>                             method subjects raters     alpha
#> "1" Krippendorff's Alpha (nominal)      250      3 0.6540881
#>                                interpretation
#> "1" Insufficient agreement - discard variable
res$gwetGroup$gwetTable$asDF               # Gwet's AC1
#>                      method subjects raters coefficient      se ci_lower
#> "1" Gwet's AC1 (unweighted)      250      3     0.69976 0.03545     0.63
#>     ci_upper           p
#> "1"     0.77 7.61843e-53
res$allPairsKappaTable$asDF                # Cohen's kappa for every pair
#>       rater_a rater_b   n  peragree     kappa         se  ci_lower  ci_upper
#> "1_2" Rater 1 Rater 2 249 0.9196787 0.8205535 0.03832152 0.7454447 0.8956623
#> "1_3" Rater 1 Rater 3 249 0.8433735 0.6661395 0.04800118 0.5720589 0.7602201
#> "2_3" Rater 2 Rater 3 250 0.7600000 0.4943707 0.05604538 0.3845237 0.6042176
#>               z             p
#> "1_2" 21.412343 1.025272e-101
#> "1_3" 13.877566  8.663573e-44
#> "2_3"  8.820899  1.135447e-18

Several tables live inside result groups, so the path has two parts (res$krippTableGroup$krippTable, res$gwetGroup$gwetTable, res$iccGroup$iccTable).

Ordinal ratings: weighted kappa

For two raters scoring an ordered scale, weighted kappa gives partial credit for near-misses. wght = "squared" (quadratic weights) is the usual choice for grades.

res_w <- agreement(
  data = histopathology,
  vars = c("Rater A", "Rater B"),
  wght = "squared"
)
res_w$irrtable$asDF
#>                   method subjects raters peragree     kappa  ci_lower  ci_upper
#> "1" Quadratic-weighted κ      250      2     58.8 0.4005073 0.2832064 0.5178081
#>            z            p
#> "1" 6.376624 1.810345e-10

Continuous measurements: ICC and Lin’s CCC 

res_c <- agreement(
  data = histopathology,
  vars = c("Measurement1", "Measurement2"),
  icc = TRUE,
  iccType = "icc21",
  linCCC = TRUE,
  blandAltmanPlot = TRUE
)
res_c$iccGroup$iccTable$asDF
#>                                 model subjects raters icc_value   ci_lower
#> "1" ICC(2,1) - Two-way random, single      250      2 0.1718531 0.04903747
#>      ci_upper  f_value df1 df2           p
#> "1" 0.2895482 1.414754 249 249 0.003187137
res_c$iccGroup$linCCCTable$asDF
#>                         comparison subjects       ccc   ci_lower  ci_upper
#> "1_2" Measurement1 vs Measurement2      250 0.1712834 0.06751243 0.2713883
#>       pearson_r bias_factor   interpretation
#> "1_2" 0.2011813   0.8513884 Poor concordance

Pick the ICC model from the study design (Shrout & Fleiss 1979; McGraw & Wong 1996):

iccType Model Use when
icc11 / icc1k One-way random effects each case is rated by a different set of raters
icc21 / icc2k Two-way random effects, absolute agreement the same raters rate every case and are a sample of possible raters
icc31 / icc3k Two-way mixed effects, consistency the same fixed raters rate every case and only their ranking matters

The 1 forms give the reliability of a single rater; the k forms give the reliability of the mean of the k raters, which is always higher.

Rater clustering

raterClustering = TRUE groups raters by how alike they rate. See Diagnostic Style Clustering.

Interpreting kappa

Landis and Koch (1977) proposed these descriptive bands. They are a convention, not a validated clinical threshold; always report the confidence interval.

Kappa Landis & Koch label
< 0 Poor
0.00 - 0.20 Slight
0.21 - 0.40 Fair
0.41 - 0.60 Moderate
0.61 - 0.80 Substantial
0.81 - 1.00 Almost perfect

For the ICC, Koo and Li (2016) suggest < 0.50 poor, 0.50 - 0.75 moderate, 0.75 - 0.90 good and > 0.90 excellent, judged on the 95% confidence interval.

Kappa depends on prevalence: with one very common category, kappa can be low while percent agreement is high (the “kappa paradox”). Report percent agreement alongside kappa, and consider Gwet’s AC1 or PABAK.

Sample size

To plan an agreement study, use the kappa sample-size tools under jamovi’s Power menu: kappaSizeCI(), kappaSizePower() and kappaSizeFixedN().

References

  • Landis JR, Koch GG. The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data. Biometrics. 1977;33:159-174.
  • Shrout PE, Fleiss JL. Intraclass correlations: uses in assessing rater reliability. Psychol Bull. 1979;86:420-428.
  • McGraw KO, Wong SP. Forming inferences about some intraclass correlation coefficients. Psychol Methods. 1996;1:30-46.
  • Koo TK, Li MY. A guideline of selecting and reporting intraclass correlation coefficients for reliability research. J Chiropr Med. 2016;15:155-163.
  • Gwet KL. Computing inter-rater reliability and its variance in the presence of high agreement. Br J Math Stat Psychol. 2008;61:29-48.
  • Krippendorff K. Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology. 4th ed. Sage; 2018.
